J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The challenge in this appeal is to the order dated 20.12.2019 passed
by the 1st respondent Arunachal Pradesh State Electricity Regulatory
Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) in petition no.TP-
07 of 2018 thereby approving the Aggregate Revenue Requirement (ARR)
and transmission charges for 132kV transmission system of the appellant for
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.161 of 2023 Page 2 of 9

power evacuation from appellant’s 24MW Dikshi Small Hydro Electric Project
for the Financial Year (FY) 2019-20, 2020-21 and 20212-22.
2. The appellant is a transmission licensee having been granted the
license under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003 by the Commission for
carrying on the business of transmission of electrical energy through 132kV
transmission line from Diksha sub-station to 132kV Tenga sub-station, S/C
132kV Tenga Switching Station to Nechipu LILO connection, D/C located in
West Kameng District of Arunachal Pradesh.
3. A Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) dated 17.03.2011 was signed by
the appellant with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh for implementation
of the above transmission project on BOOT basis. The appellant received
Letter of Comfort dated on 22.02.2016 from the Chief Engineer for
transmission connectivity to connect to the existing 132kV line at an
intermediate location close to transmission line alignment for the project. In
order to connect to the Balipara-Khupi 132kV line the appellant had to
undertake following transmission system, which is the subject matter of the
instant appeal: -
132 kV Single Circuit Line 10.5 KM
132 kV Double Circuit Line 21.5 KM
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.161 of 2023 Page 3 of 9

Number of Bays at 132 kV Switching Substation Tenga 4 Nos.
4. The appellant got the estimated cost of the project evaluated by the
Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (PGCIL) on 11.04.2017 on the basis
of cost of transmission system at the price levels prevailing in December,
2016. Thereafter work contract was given by the appellant to
M/s PK Thungon Builders Pvt. Ltd on 06.06.2016 for a part of the 132kV line
for value of Rs.26.69 crores. Thereafter an agreement dated 01.07.2017
was executed between the appellant and M/s PK Thungon Builders Pvt. Ltd.
for supply of balance material for the transmission line and Switching Station
for an amount of Rs.23.63 crores.
5. The appellant was granted transmission license with respect to the
said transmission system on 12.07.2018.
6. A Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) was signed between the
appellant and the 2nd respondent i.e. the Department of Power, Government
of Arunachal Pradesh on 16.10.2018 for sale of power from the power project
of the appellant through the said transmission line with the following clauses
relating to the transmission connectivity: -
“4.0 EVACUATION OF POWER AND METERING:
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.161 of 2023 Page 4 of 9

4.1 The entire Power from Dikshi HEP shall be delivered at
Interconnection Point and will be transmitted through Dikshi-
Tenga-Nechipu 132 KV transmission line connected to
existing Balipara- Khuppi 132 KV line near Nechipu (LILO
Connection). The Generating Company shall be responsible
for developing the evacuation system for the Project and
shall subject to the provisions of the MoA signed between
the Generating Company and the Government of Arunachal
Pradesh.
4.2 The DoPAP shall pay the Transmission Charges as
determined by APSERC to the Generating Company
/Transmission Licensee for the Transmission System
beyond the Interconnection Point upto LILO Connection till
such time the ownership of such Transmission Lines/System
remains with the Company/Transmission Licensee.
Generating Company/Transmission Licensee”
7. Thereafter, the appellant filed the tariff petition bearing no.TP-07 of
2018 before the Commission seeking approval of ARR and transmission
charges for the said transmission system for the FYs 2019-20, 2020-21, and
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.161 of 2023 Page 5 of 9

2021-22 as per Arunachal Pradesh State Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Multi-Year Tariff Regulations) Regulations, 2018. The petition has been
disposed of by the Commission vide impugned order dated 20.12.2019
thereby approving the capital cost of the transmission project as Rs.50.7
crores and the total IDC as Rs.9.05 crores.
8. Aggrieved by certain findings of the Commission in the impugned
order, the instant appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
9. We have heard Ms. Swapna Seshadri, learned counsel for the
appellant and Ms. Archana Maharaj, learned counsel for the respondent
Commission. We have also perused the impugned order of the Commission
and have gone through the written submissions filed by the learned counsels.
10. The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the Commission
has adopted a pick and choose method in the impugned order by restricting
the cost of civil works of the project to Rs.50.70 crores as against the
appellant’s claimed expenditure of Rs.63.58 crores. She further submitted
that the Commission has erred in restricting the IDC to Rs.9.05 crores as
against the appellant’s claim of Rs.11.36 crores, despite holding that the
appellant is not liable to be penalized for time overrun.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.161 of 2023 Page 6 of 9

11. The learned counsel pointed out that the Commission has restricted
the cost of civil works by comparing the contract rates, rates as per the
Detailed Project Report (DPR) of PGCIL and the actual cost incurred by the
appellant, thereupon adopting the lower of the three, which is arbitrary and
without any basis. She would argue that the Commission has failed to apply
the principle of prudence check on the cost incurred towards civil works by
the appellant and has simply taken different cost parameters for reference
and adopted the lowest of them, which is absolutely contrary to the
methodology envisaged under Regulation 4.3 of the APSERC (Multi Year
Tariff) Regulations, 2018 and does not fall within the ambit of “prudence
check” as envisaged under the regulatory framework. She submitted that
the project cost as per the DPR of PGCIL was arrived at by considering the
cost of transmission system with the price levels prevailing in December,
2016 and which would naturally have been on lower side in comparison to
the price levels prevailing in the subsequent years. It is also her submission
on the comparison of costs incurred by the appellant that the costs specified
by PGCIL in its DPR is also arbitrary for the reason that PGCIL is a public
sector enterprise engaged largely in the business of transmission, enjoys
economies of large scale and volume across the country. She pointed out
that the restrictions in the costs of civil works have also resulted in reduced
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.161 of 2023 Page 7 of 9

IDC despite the entire time overruns that have been condoned by the
Commission.
12. Even though, the contentions/submissions advanced on behalf of the
appellant were sought to be refuted by the learned counsel for the
respondent Commission, yet, after advancing arguments for some time, the
learned counsel, upon instructions, stated that the case may be remanded
back to the Commission for reconsideration. In the written submissions filed
on behalf of the Commission also, in Paragraph 27, in addition to the prayer
for dismissal of the appeal, it has been prayed that any such order as this
Tribunal deems fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case may
be passed.
13. Having regard to the submissions of the appellant’s counsel, as noted
hereinabove, and in view of such clear-cut statement on behalf of the
Commission during the hearing of the appeal and considering the above
noted prayer made in the written submissions, we find it appropriate to
remand the matter back to the Commission for fresh consideration on the
issues raised in this appeal by the appellant, as noted hereinabove.
14. Accordingly, we hereby, set aside the impugned order of the
Commission to the extent assailed in this appeal and remand the matter back
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.161 of 2023 Page 8 of 9

to the Commission for fresh consideration on the issues noted hereinabove,
after affording reasonable opportunity of hearing to the parties. The
Commission shall endeavor to conclude such exercise within three months
from today.
15. The appeal stands allowed, albeit to the extent mentioned
hereinabove. All pending IAs, if any, also stand disposed of.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 05th day of October, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. This appeal is directed against the order dated 20.12.2019 passed by
Arunachal Pradesh State Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter
referred to as “the Commission”) in appellant’s petition no.TP-06 of 2018
whereby project specific tariff of the appellant’s Dikshi Small Hydro Electric
Project (24MW) was determined by the Commission.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.160 of 2023 Page 2 of 8

2. The facts of the case, stated briefly, are that the appellant had entered
into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Government of
Arunachal Pradesh on 17.03.2011 for development of the above noted
Hydro Electric Project. Accordingly, the appellant submitted a Detailed
Project Report (DPR) on 14.04.2012 and obtained techno-electric clearance
on 10.06.2013.
3. Thereafter, the appellant awarded civil construction work to M/s PK
Thungon Builders and entered into an initial contract dated 06.08.2014 with
regards to the same. Subsequently, a renegotiated contract dated
01.06.2015 was also entered into by the appellant with the contractor
containing revised contractual rates. It needs mention here that the
renegotiated contract mentioned reduced rates for certain components of the
power project.
4. Vide communication dated 01.03.2018, the Department of Power,
Government of Arunachal Pradesh expressed its willingness to buy power of
the said power project of the appellant. In pursuance thereto, a Power
Purchase Agreement (PPA) was executed between the appellant and
Department of Power, Government of Arunachal Pradesh (2nd respondent)
on 25.07.2018.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.160 of 2023 Page 3 of 8

5. The project was subsequently commissioned on 19.09.2019.
6. Meanwhile, the petition no.TP-06 of 2018 came to be filed by the
appellant before the Commission seeking determination of tariff for the said
hydroelectric power project, from its proposed date of commercial operation
as per the Arunachal Pradesh State Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Terms and Conditions for Tariff Determination from Renewable Energy
Sources) Regulations, 2018, for a period of 35 years. The petition has been
disposed of by the Commission vide impugned order dated 20.12.2019
thereby approving the capital cost of the project and determining the
generation tariff for the same for supply of power to the 2nd respondent for a
period of 35 years for distribution in the State of Arunachal Pradesh.
7. Aggrieved by certain findings of the Commission in the impugned tariff
order, the instant appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
8. The main grounds upon which the appellant has assailed the
impugned order of the Commission are that the Commission, while
determining the tariff for the appellant’s power project has:
(a) adopted a pick and choose method in restricting the cost of civil
works to Rs.182.78 crs., as against the Appellant’s claimed
expenditure of Rs.235.91 crs. Consequently, despite holding that
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.160 of 2023 Page 4 of 8

the Appellant is not liable to be penalized for time overrun, the
Commission has restricted the Interest During Construction (“IDC”)
at Rs.41.78 crs. on the admitted hard cost, as against the
Appellant’s claim of Rs.52.63 crs.;
(b) failed to consider and allow the additional cost impact of the 3 floods
encountered by the Appellant during the construction of the Project,
on the singular reasoning that the insurance company had settled
the corresponding claims of the Appellant for a lesser amount; and
(c) erroneously factored in and deducted subsidy amount of Rs.5 crs.
from the capital cost of the Project, despite the Appellant not having
received such subsidy from the Ministry of New and Renewable
Energy (MNRE).
9. We have heard Ms. Swapna Seshadri, learned counsel for the
appellant and Ms. Archana Maharaj, learned counsel for the respondent
Commission. We have also perused the impugned order of the Commission
and have gone through the written submissions filed by the learned counsels.
10. The submissions of the learned counsel for the appellant can be
conveniently divided under the following three heads: -
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.160 of 2023 Page 5 of 8

(I) Reduction in cost of civil works:
It is submitted by the learned counsel for the appellant that the
Commission has erroneously allowed only Rs.182.78 crores
towards cost of civil works against the claim of the appellant to
the tune of Rs.235.91 crores. It is submitted that the Commission
has restricted the hard cost to the lower of the cost of each
component between the original and negotiated contract entered
into by the appellant with the contractor, which is arbitrary and
without any basis.
(II) Disallowance of the increase in costs due to three floods:
The learned counsel for the appellant would submit that the
Commission has erroneously disallowed the amount incurred in
restoration of damage to the power project on account of floods,
solely on the ground that the insurance company had settled the
claim of the appellant for a lower amount without considering the
actual loss suffered by the appellant and actual cost incurred by
the appellant on the restoration work.
(III) Deduction of subsidy amount from the capital cost:
It is submitted by the learned counsel for the appellant that the
Commission has erroneously deducted Rs.5 crores from the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.160 of 2023 Page 6 of 8

capital cost despite the fact that the appellant had not received
any such amount as subsidy from the Ministry of New and
Renewable Energy (MNRE).
11. Even though, the contentions/submissions advanced on behalf of the
appellant were sought to be refuted by the learned counsel for the
respondent Commission, yet, after advancing arguments for some time, the
learned counsel, upon instructions, stated that the case may be remanded
back to the Commission for reconsideration. In the written submissions filed
on behalf of the Commission also it has been stated in Paragraph no.34 that
the case may be remanded back to the Commission for reconsideration.
12. Having regard to the submissions of the appellant’s counsel and in
view of such clear-cut statement on behalf of the Commission during the
hearing of the appeal as well as in the written submissions, we find it
appropriate to remand the matter back to the Commission for fresh
consideration on the issues raised in this appeal by the appellant, as noted
hereinabove.
13. Accordingly, we hereby, set aside the impugned order of the
Commission to the extent assailed in this appeal and remand the matter back
to the Commission for fresh consideration on the issues noted hereinabove,
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.160 of 2023 Page 7 of 8

after affording reasonable opportunity of hearing to the parties. The
Commission shall endeavor to conclude such exercise within three months
from today.
14. The appeal stands allowed, albeit to the extent mentioned
hereinabove. All pending IAs, if any, also stand disposed of.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 05th day of October, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

COURT-1
IN THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL FOR ELECTRICITY
(Appellate Jurisdiction)
IA Nos. 1596 & 1035 of 2025
in
DFR No. 243 of 2025
Dated : 5th October, 2026
Present : Hon`ble Ms. Seema Gupta, Officiating Chairperson
Hon`ble Mr. Virender Bhat, Judicial Member
In the matter of:
Abundant Energy Private Limited .... Appellant(s)
Versus
Punjab State Power Corporation Limited & Ors. .... Respondent(s)
Counsel on record for the Appellant(s) : Tajender K. Joshi
Rampal Kohle
for App. 1
Counsel on record for the Respondent(s) : Suparna Srivastava
for Res. 1
Aadil Singh Boparai
for Res. 2
Gargi Kumar
for Res. 3
ORDER
IA No. 1596 of 2025
(For condonation of delay in refiling the Appeal)
1. Considering the rival submissions made by the Learned
Counsels and taking note of the averments made in the application,
delay in refiling the appeal is hereby condoned.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No.1596 of 2025 in DFR 243 of 2025 Page 1 of 7

IA No. 1035 of 2025
(For condonation of delay in filing the appeal)
2. Delay in filing the instant appeal is sought to be condoned by
way of this application.
3. The appellant was, in pursuance to the Request for Proposal
(RFP) dated 24th December, 2014 issued by 2nd Respondent – Punjab
Electricity Development Authority (PEDA) for development of 250 MW
capacity grid connected solar PV Power Projects, allotted 1 MW Solar
PV Power Project to be set up in District Tarn Taran, Punjab with an
approved tariff of Rs.7.68/ per kwh after providing a discount of four
paisa on the generic tariff of Rs.7.72/ kwh.
4. Subsequently, Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated
31.03.2015 was executed with between the Appellant and first
Respondent – Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. (PSPCL). The
scheduled date of Commissioning (SCOD) of the project was 10 months
from the date of signing of the PPA. However, the project could not be
commissioned by its SCOD and accordingly the Appellant approached
the 3rd Respondent – Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission
(hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) with petition No. 25 of
2016 for extension of SCOD. The petition came to be disposed of vide
order dated 14.02.2107 thereby refusing to extend the SCOD and
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No.1596 of 2025 in DFR 243 of 2025 Page 2 of 7

further reducing the tariff of the project from Rs.7.69/kwh to
Rs.5.39/kwh.
5. The Appellant filed a Review Petition before the Commission for
review of the said order dated 14.02.2017 which was allowed by the
Commission vide order dated 21.05.2018. Accordingly, the SCOD of the
project was extended upto 23.08.2016. The first Respondent – PSPCL
assailed the Review Order dated 21.05.2018 before this Tribunal by way
of Appeal No. 316 of 2018. The Appeal was allowed by this Tribunal
vide judgement dated 28.08.2024 thereby setting aside the review order
dated 21.05.2018 and restoring the order dated 14.02.2017.
6. The instant appeal has now been filed by the Appellant against
the order dated 14.02.2017 on 07.07.2025, with a delay of 3020 days.
7. We have heard the Learned Senior Counsel, Shri Sanjay Sen for
the Appellant, Ms. Suparna Shrivastava, Learned Counsel for first
Respondent and Ms. Gargi Kumar, Learned Counsel for the 3rd
Respondent. We have also perused the written submission filed by the
Learned Counsel.
8. As noted hereinabove, the Appellant had sought review of the
order dated 14.02.2017 (which is impugned in this appeal) before the
Commission by way of Review Petition No. 04 of 2017 which came to
be allowed by the Commission vide order dated 21.05.2018. Thus, the
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No.1596 of 2025 in DFR 243 of 2025 Page 3 of 7

grievance of the appellant stood addressed by the said review order as
its claim for extension of SCOD of its solar power project was extended.
However, the said review order was later on set aside by this Tribunal
vide judgement dated 28.08.2024 in Appeal No. 316 of 2018 filed by
first Respondent PSPCL.
9. Evidently, therefore, the Appellant got reason or occasion to
assail the order dated 14.02.2017 on 28.08.2024 when the same was
restored by the Tribunal vide the judgement passed in Appeal No. 316
of 2018. Till then, the review order dated 21.05.2018 was in force which
was in favour of the Appellant.
10. In these circumstances, period of delay must be reckoned from
28.08.2024 as prior to the said date, there was no cause or occasion for
the Appellant to approach this Tribunal, the order dated 14.02.2017
having been set aside in the review proceedings.
11. The period of delay, when reckoned from 28.08.2024, comes to
332 days, which is less than a year.
12. It is argued on behalf of the Respondents that no sufficient reason
has been shown by the Appellant for condoning the delay of 332 days
also. The learned Counsels for the Respondents argued that the
Appellant had knowledge of the judgement dated 28.08.2024 of the
Tribunal on that very day itself as the same was pronounced in open
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No.1596 of 2025 in DFR 243 of 2025 Page 4 of 7

court and Appellant had also received a copy of the judgement on
26.09.2024. It is submitted that prolonged internal deliberations and
multiple legal opinions, as projected by the Appellant, do not constitute
“sufficient cause”. According to the Learned Counsels, the delay in filing
the Appeal cannot be condoned as it fails the test of “sufficient cause”
as laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in various judgement
namely P.K. Ramachandran Vs. State of Kerala & Anr. (1997) 7 SCC
556 (para 3.6); Baswaraj & Anr. Vs. Special Land Acquisition Officer
(2013) 14 SCC 81 (para 9); State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Ram Kumar
Chaudhary (2024) SCC Online SC 3612, (Para 7) and Sushil Kumar
Sen vs. State of Bihar (1975) 1 SCC 774.
13. With regards to these submissions on behalf of the Respondents,
we may note that this Tribunal has been consistently condoning the
delay of upto one year in filing appeals, albeit upon imposition of suitable
costs commensurate with the period of delay. This is primarily for the
reason that this Tribunal is a National Tribunal having its seat in New
Delhi and the litigants from the farthest corners of India have to traverse
considerable distances to reach here, consult the lawyers and to get the
appeal drafted as well as filed. We find it unjustified to avoid denying an
opportunity of having their appeals adjudicated on merits, to such
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No.1596 of 2025 in DFR 243 of 2025 Page 5 of 7

litigants. This Tribunal being the forum of first appeal, which is a
statutory right for the litigant against whom the order is passed by the
Regulatory Commission, must endeavour to decide the appeal on
merits instead of throwing out the appeals on technicalities unless the
delay appears to be contumacious and deliberate. That is not the case
in the present appeal.
14. Thus, considering the overall facts & circumstances of the case
as well as the above noted practice being followed consistently by this
Tribunal, we are of the opinion that the delay in the instant case also,
which is 332 days, should be condemned subject payment of cost.
15. Hence, the application is allowed and the delay in filing the appeal
is condoned subject to payment of Rs.1.5 lac as costs to be deposited
with CTUIL within three weeks from today. Proof of deposit of cost be
filed within two weeks thereafter. The Appellant shall also intimate CTU
of the Appeal No. and date of order, in terms of which cost are paid.
16. Needless to state that in case aforesaid cost are not paid and
proof of payment is not submitted within the stipulated time, the
application for condonation of delay in filing the appeal shall stand
dismissed automatically and the Appeal shall stand rejected.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No.1596 of 2025 in DFR 243 of 2025 Page 6 of 7

DFR No : 243 of 2025 & IA No. 1036 OF 2025
17. The Respondents shall file reply to the appeal as well as the
interim application within four weeks. Rejoinder be filed by the Appellant
within two weeks thereafter.
18. List on 18.11.2026.
Pronounced in the open court on this 5th day of October, 2026.
Virender Bhat Seema Gupta
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson
